unit.title: Terminate basic signal and data cables

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A screened (shielded) signal cable has a bare drain wire. Where should the screen be connected?

essays.stem: Describe the hazards when terminating signal and data cables, and say how you would control each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Some data cables carry power to devices such as cameras and phones, and telephone lines carry a ringing voltage that can give a shock, so I unplug or disconnect the cable at both ends, or have the circuit isolated, before I work on it. Short, sharp off-cuts of copper can fly into the eyes when I trim conductors, so I wear safety glasses and point the cut away from people. The blades in strippers and punch-down tools can cut hands, so I use the right tool and keep my fingers clear. Work above ceilings is work at height, so I use a sound stepladder that is set up properly. Cables on the floor are trip hazards, so I keep them tidy. Mains cables may run near data cables, so I treat them as live and do not disturb them.
markingPoints: Power on data cables and telephone ringing voltage: disconnect or isolate first
Flying off-cuts: safety glasses and cutting away from people
Sharp blades: right tool, fingers clear
Work at height: sound stepladder set up properly
Trips and nearby mains cables: keep tidy and treat mains as live

essays.stem: Compare twisted-pair data cable and coaxial cable. Describe how each one is made, and give one use for each.
essays.modelAnswer: Twisted-pair cable, such as Cat 5e or Cat 6, has eight thin insulated conductors twisted into four pairs inside an outer jacket. Each pair has a solid colour and a white-striped partner: blue, orange, green and brown. The twists cut down interference and crosstalk, and some types also have a foil screen. It is terminated with RJ45 plugs, keystone jacks or patch panels, and is used for computer networks, phones and network cameras. Coaxial cable has one centre conductor, surrounded by an insulating dielectric, then a foil and braid screen, and then an outer jacket. All the layers share the same centre, which is why it is called coaxial. It is terminated with F-type or BNC connectors, and is used for satellite and cable TV and for some CCTV cameras.
markingPoints: Twisted pair: eight conductors in four coloured, twisted pairs in a jacket
Twists (and any screen) reduce interference and crosstalk
Twisted pair: RJ45 connectors; used for networks, phones or cameras
Coax: centre conductor, dielectric, foil and braid screen, jacket
Coax: F-type or BNC connectors; used for TV, satellite or CCTV

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to make a straight-through Cat 6 patch lead with RJ45 plugs.
essays.modelAnswer: I cut the cable to length and, if the plugs have boots, slide a boot onto each end first. I strip a short length of outer jacket with a cable stripper, as the plug maker says, taking care not to nick the pairs, and I cut off the ripcord. I untwist the pairs only as much as I need and straighten the conductors. I arrange them in the T568B order: white-orange, orange, white-green, blue, white-blue, green, white-brown, brown. I trim the ends straight and even, short enough that the jacket will go inside the plug. I push the conductors into the plug, keeping the order, until every one reaches the end, and check the order by eye. I crimp the plug with the correct crimp tool. I make the other end the same way, with the same T568B order, then test the lead and label it.
markingPoints: Fits boots first and strips the jacket without nicking the pairs
Untwists as little as possible and puts conductors in T568B order
Trims evenly so the jacket goes inside the plug and all conductors reach the end
Crimps with the correct tool and die
Same code at both ends; tests and labels the lead

essays.stem: Describe how to terminate a twisted-pair cable onto a keystone jack using a punch-down tool.
essays.modelAnswer: I strip the outer jacket back only as far as I need, without nicking the pairs, and cut off the ripcord. I check which colour code the job uses, A or B, and look at the colour labels on the jack. I lay each pair into its slots, keeping the twists as close to the slots as possible and the jacket close to the back of the jack. I put the jack in a holder so that it is well supported. I place the punch-down tool on each conductor with the cutting edge on the outside, towards the spare end, and push firmly until it clicks. The tool seats the conductor in the slot, which cuts through the insulation, and it trims off the spare end. I check that every conductor is fully seated, fit the cap if there is one, clip the jack into the faceplate and test the link.
markingPoints: Strips only as much jacket as needed without damage
Follows the job's colour code using the labels on the jack
Keeps twists and jacket close to the termination
Punches down with the cutting edge facing out until it clicks
Checks seating, fits cap and faceplate, and tests

essays.stem: Describe how to fit a compression F-type connector to an RG6 coaxial cable.
essays.modelAnswer: I cut the end of the cable square with a cable cutter. I set a coax stripper for RG6 and for the connector I am using, and turn it around the cable to strip it in two steps: one length shows the bare centre conductor, and the next shows the dielectric with the jacket removed. I check that the centre conductor is not nicked and that no foil or braid strands touch it. I fold the braid back neatly over the jacket, as the connector maker says. I push the connector onto the cable until the dielectric is level with the inside of the connector and the centre conductor sticks out just past the front. Then I put the connector in the compression tool and squeeze until it closes fully. Finally I check it by eye and test the lead for continuity and for shorts.
markingPoints: Cuts square and uses a stripper set for the cable and connector
Centre conductor undamaged; no braid or foil strands touching it
Braid folded back as the maker says
Connector pushed fully on; centre conductor just past the front
Compresses fully with the right tool and tests for continuity and shorts

essays.stem: Explain how data cables should be handled and supported during installation so that they work well. Include bends, ties and power cables.
essays.modelAnswer: Data cable must be pulled gently, because stretching it can loosen the twists in the pairs and spoil its performance. I pull it from a box or reel that turns freely, so that it does not kink. I keep bends gentle and never kink or crush the cable; the smallest bend allowed is given by the cable maker. I support long runs on hooks, trays or in trunking, so the cable does not hang on its own weight. I use hook-and-loop straps, or cable ties fitted only snugly, so the jacket is not squeezed. I keep data cables apart from mains power cables along the run, and where they must cross, I cross them at a right angle. I keep cables away from heat and sharp edges, leave a small neat loop at each end, and label both ends.
markingPoints: Pulls gently from a free-turning reel; no stretching or kinks
Gentle bends within the maker's limit
Supports runs and uses snug ties or hook-and-loop straps
Keeps apart from mains power and crosses at a right angle
Avoids heat and sharp edges, leaves a loop, labels both ends

essays.stem: Describe how you would test a newly made data cable, and what faults the tester can show.
essays.modelAnswer: I connect one end of the cable to the main unit of a cable tester and the other end to the remote unit; for a patch lead, both ends can plug into the same tester. I switch on, run the test and read the wire map on the screen or lights. A good straight-through cable shows pins 1 to 8 each joining the same pin at the far end, in order. The tester can show an open, where a conductor is broken or not connected, and a short, where two conductors touch. It can also show a reversed pair, where the two wires of a pair are swapped, and crossed pairs, where pairs are on the wrong pins. Better testers also find split pairs, where the pins match but the pairs are mixed. I record the result with the cable label and remake any cable that fails.
markingPoints: Connects the main and remote units correctly and runs the test
Knows what a good wire map looks like
Opens and shorts
Reversed, crossed and split pairs
Records results and remakes failed cables

essays.stem: Explain the T568A and T568B colour codes, and say when you would use a straight-through lead or a crossover lead.
essays.modelAnswer: T568A and T568B are two standard orders for the eight conductors in an RJ45 plug or jack. In T568B the order from pin 1 to pin 8 is: white-orange, orange, white-green, blue, white-blue, green, white-brown, brown. T568A is the same except that the orange and green pairs swap places, so it starts white-green, green, white-orange. The blue pair is always on pins 4 and 5, and the brown pair on pins 7 and 8. A job should use one code throughout, as the specification says. A straight-through lead has the same code at both ends, and is used to connect a computer, phone or camera to an outlet or switch. A crossover lead has T568A at one end and T568B at the other. It was used to join two computers or two switches directly; most modern equipment now sorts this out by itself.
markingPoints: Explains that A and B are standard conductor orders
Gives the T568B order correctly
T568A swaps the orange and green pairs; one code used throughout a job
Straight-through: same code both ends; connects devices to outlets or switches
Crossover: A one end, B the other; for direct device-to-device links

essays.stem: Why are labelling and test records important for data cabling? Describe a good labelling system.
essays.modelAnswer: A building may have hundreds of data cables that all look the same. Labels let anyone find which outlet goes to which port on the patch panel, so faults can be found quickly and changes made without unplugging the wrong cable. Test records prove that each cable passed when it was installed, which protects the installer and helps with later fault-finding. A good labelling system gives every cable a unique number, made from the room, the outlet and the port, for example 2A-04. The same number is put on both ends of the cable, on the faceplate and on the patch panel port. Labels should be printed, not hand-written, and must not rub off. The numbers are also written on the as-built drawing and in the test record for each cable.
markingPoints: Labels let outlets and panel ports be matched quickly
Test records prove each link passed at installation and help fault-finding
Each cable gets a unique number (for example room, outlet, port)
Same number on both ends, faceplate and panel port
Printed, lasting labels; numbers on drawings and test records

essays.stem: Describe how to terminate a multi-core screened signal cable, for example for an alarm or intercom, at screw terminals.
essays.modelAnswer: With the system switched off or disconnected, I check the drawing or the maker's instructions to see which core goes to which terminal. I strip the outer jacket back only as far as I need, without cutting the cores or the screen. I fold back or trim the foil screen and gather the drain wire, as the instructions say. I strip each core to the length the terminal needs. Where the cores are stranded, I fit a bootlace ferrule of the right size with the crimp tool. I connect each core to its terminal, tighten the screw and give it a gentle tug. I connect the screen or drain wire only where the drawing says, often at one end only, and sleeve it so it cannot touch other terminals. I label the cable, record the colours used and test each core for continuity.
markingPoints: Works with the system off and follows the drawing or maker's instructions
Strips jacket and cores without damage to the right length
Fits ferrules of the right size on stranded cores and tightens terminals
Connects the screen or drain only where the drawing says, and sleeves it
Labels, records colours and tests continuity

practical1.title: Make and test twisted-pair patch leads and terminate data outlets
practical1.brief: Each member makes one straight-through patch lead about 2 m long, with T568B RJ45 plugs and boots at both ends. Then each member terminates one length of Cat 6 cable onto a keystone jack with the punch-down tool, clips it into a faceplate on the training board, and terminates the other end of the same cable onto a port of the training patch panel. The group tests every patch lead and every outlet-to-panel link with a cable tester, remakes any that fail, labels both ends with the agreed numbers and fills in a test record. No cable is plugged into a live network switch or any powered equipment. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when all the links pass and the area is clean.
materials: RJ45 plugs and boots to suit the cable
Keystone jacks, faceplates and a training patch panel on a board
Cable stripper, side cutters, RJ45 crimp tool and punch-down tool
Cable tester (wire map) with remote unit
Labels or a label printer, and a test record form
photos: Each member's cable end stripped, with the pairs untwisted only a little
Conductors in T568B order before they go into the plug
A crimped plug showing all eight conductors at the end and the jacket inside
A keystone jack punched down, with the twists kept close to the slots
The patch panel port punched down, seen from the back
The cable tester showing a pass on a link
Labels on both ends, on the faceplate and on the panel
The completed test record and the tidy work area
checklist: Stripped the jacket without nicking the pairs
Kept the untwisted length as short as possible
Put the conductors in the correct T568B order at both ends
Jacket inside the plug and every conductor at the end before crimping
Punched down each conductor fully with the cutting edge facing out
Tested each lead and link, found any fault and remade it
Labelled both ends with the same unique number and filled in the test record
Wore safety glasses when trimming and kept the area clear of off-cuts
safety: Do not connect any lead to a live network switch, telephone line or powered device during the task
Wear safety glasses when cutting and trimming conductors
Keep fingers clear of the blades in strippers and the punch-down tool
Pick up small off-cuts at once so nobody slips or steps on them
Follow the tool maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Terminate and test coaxial cables and a screened signal cable
practical2.brief: Each member makes one RG6 coaxial lead about 1.5 m long with a compression F-type connector at each end, and fits a BNC connector to each end of a short RG59 lead, as used for CCTV. Then the group terminates a 4-core screened alarm or intercom cable between two terminal strips on the training board, as the assessor's drawing shows: one member prepares each end, and every member terminates at least one core with a bootlace ferrule. Test every coax lead with a multimeter for continuity of the centre conductor and of the screen, and for no short between them. Test each core of the signal cable for continuity. Label every cable and record the results. No cable is connected to a dish, TV, camera or any powered equipment. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Compression F-type connectors and BNC connectors to suit the cables
Coax stripper set for each cable, cable cutter and compression tool
4-core screened signal cable, two terminal strips on a training board, and the assessor's drawing
Bootlace ferrules and a ferrule crimp tool
Multimeter, labels and a test record form
photos: A coax end stripped, showing the centre conductor, dielectric and folded braid
An F-type connector pushed on, before compression
The finished F-type lead after compression
A finished BNC connector on the RG59 lead
The signal cable stripped, showing the cores, screen and drain wire
Cores with ferrules fitted in the terminal strip
A multimeter continuity test on a lead
Labels, the test record and the tidy work area
checklist: Cut the coax square and stripped it with the correct stripper setting
No braid or foil strands touching the centre conductor
Fitted and compressed the F-type and BNC connectors as the maker says
Stripped the signal cable without cutting the cores or the screen
Fitted ferrules of the right size and terminated cores to the terminals on the drawing
Connected the screen or drain wire only where the drawing says, and sleeved it
Tested each lead and core for continuity and shorts, and recorded the results
Labelled every cable and left the work area tidy
safety: Do not connect any cable to a dish, receiver, camera or other powered equipment during the task
Wear safety glasses when cutting coax braid and trimming cores
Keep fingers clear of the stripper blades and cut away from your body
Pick up braid strands and off-cuts at once; they are sharp
Follow the tool maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
